people.name: Gaius Atilius Regulus Serranus
people.summary: Consul 257, when he rushed ahead of his fleet off Tyndaris and was nearly caught before winning the battle, and again 250, when with Manlius Vulso he opened the siege of Lilybaeum. The cognomen Serranus was later explained by the tale that he was found sowing (serere) when called to office.

people.name: Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus
people.summary: Regulus' colleague in 256, commanding the third and fourth squadrons at Ecnomus. After the landing at Aspis he was recalled with most of the fleet, 27,000 prisoners and the booty, leaving Regulus 15,500 men; he triumphed for the naval victory. Consul again 250 at the siege of Lilybaeum.

people.name: Servius Fulvius Paetinus Nobilior
people.summary: Consul 255 who with Marcus Aemilius Paullus took 350 ships to rescue the survivors of Regulus' army, won off Cape Hermaeum, and then lost most of the fleet in the storm off Camarina. Both consuls nonetheless triumphed for the naval victory in 254.

people.name: Marcus Aemilius Paullus
people.summary: Consul 255, victor with Fulvius Nobilior off Cape Hermaeum and survivor of the Camarina disaster. He triumphed in January 254 and a column with ships' beaks was set up on the Capitol in his honour; it was struck by lightning and destroyed in 172 (Livy 42.20).

people.name: Lucius Junius Pullus
people.summary: Consul 249 whose huge supply convoy was destroyed by Carthalo and a storm off Pachynus. Undaunted, he seized the summit of Mount Eryx and the town below. Tradition paired him with Claudius Pulcher as consuls who ignored the sacred chickens; Cicero says he killed himself rather than face trial.

people.name: Quintus Valerius Falto
people.summary: Praetor 241 who commanded the fleet at the Aegates while the consul Lutatius Catulus lay wounded. He claimed the triumph; the dispute went to a formal sponsio before the judge Atilius Calatinus, who ruled for the consul, but Falto was allowed his own naval triumph. Consul 239.

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 242 and flamen Martialis. When he wished to go to Sicily, the pontifex maximus Lucius Caecilius Metellus forbade him to leave Rome and neglect his priesthood, an early documented clash between religious and military duty. Censor 234.

people.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus
people.summary: Consul 235, when he subdued Sardinia and closed the doors of Janus for the first time since Numa, and 224, when he invaded the Boii. In 216 he argued against ransoming the Cannae prisoners; in 215 he crushed Hampsicora's Sardinian revolt. Famous for old-fashioned severity.

people.name: Gaius Atilius Regulus
people.summary: Consul 225 who brought his army back from Sardinia, landed at Pisae, and blundered into the Gallic host at Telamon from the north, trapping it against Papus' army. He was killed leading the cavalry for the hill and his head was carried to the Gallic kings.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Papus
people.summary: Consul 225 who shadowed the Gallic army down Etruria and, with Regulus arriving from the north, destroyed it at Telamon; he then ravaged the Boian country and triumphed, hanging Gallic standards and torques on the Capitol. Censor 220 with Gaius Flaminius.

people.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus
people.summary: Consul 229 who took 200 ships across the Adriatic in the First Illyrian War, received Corcyra from Demetrius of Pharos, relieved Epidamnus and Issa and celebrated a naval triumph over the Illyrians in 228.

people.name: Lucius Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 234 and 229 (when he led the land army into Illyria) and praetor 216, sent to hold the Gauls. In the Litana forest the Boii cut the trees to topple on his column; he was killed and his skull, gilded, became a sacred drinking cup in a Boian temple. He had already been elected consul for 215.
people.death: killed in the Litana forest ambush

people.name: Publius Furius Philus
people.summary: Consul 223 with Flaminius, defeating the Insubres; praetor 216, wounded at sea off Africa. As censor in 214 he and Marcus Atilius Regulus degraded those who had talked of leaving Italy after Cannae; he died before the lustrum.

people.name: Gnaeus Servilius Geminus
people.summary: Flaminius' colleague in 217, whose advance cavalry under Centenius was destroyed after Trasimene. He took a fleet to raid the African coast and Cercina, then held the line in Apulia under Fabius' system, and was killed at Cannae commanding the Roman centre as proconsul.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus
people.summary: Son of the Cunctator. When his father rode up to him as consul at Suessula, he ordered the old man to dismount, to the father's pride. He recaptured Arpi in 213 by a night attack in a rainstorm. He died before his father, who gave the funeral speech.

people.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: A survivor of Cannae, praetor in Sicily 215 and Marcellus' second in command against Syracuse, where his assault on the sea walls broke on Archimedes' engines. As consul 212 he began the siege of Capua; he was mortally wounded repelling a sortie in 211.

people.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Brother of the conqueror of Capua. As praetor in Apulia in 212 he let his army fall into indiscipline and was destroyed by Hannibal near Herdonia, fleeing early. Prosecuted by a tribune on a capital charge in 211, he went into exile at Tarquinii.

people.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus Maximus
people.summary: Consul 211, who helped defend Rome during Hannibal's march to the Colline Gate. As proconsul in 210 he was trying to recover Herdonia when Hannibal caught and destroyed his army; he died with eleven military tribunes.
people.death: killed at the second battle of Herdonia

people.name: Titus Quinctius Crispinus
people.summary: Consul 208 with Marcellus; earlier famed for a duel with his Campanian guest-friend Badius at Capua (212). Wounded in the ambush near Venusia in which Marcellus died, he escaped, warned the towns that Hannibal had Marcellus' signet ring, and died of his wounds later that year.

people.name: Marcus Cornelius Cethegus
people.summary: Censor 209 though not yet consul, consul 204 and, as proconsul with Quinctilius Varus, victor over Mago in the land of the Insubres in 203. Ennius called him 'the marrow of Persuasion' (Suadai medulla), and Cicero names him the first Roman remembered as an orator.

people.name: Publius Licinius Crassus Dives
people.summary: Elected pontifex maximus in 212 though he had held no curule office, over two senior consulars; censor 210, consul 205 with Scipio, keeping Hannibal penned in Bruttium while a plague hit his army. Livy calls him handsome, rich, eloquent and learned in pontifical law. His funeral games in 183 included 120 gladiators.

people.name: Quintus Pleminius
people.summary: Scipio's legate who recaptured Locri in 205 and then plundered the city and the treasury of Persephone; he had two military tribunes flogged to death. Sent to Rome in chains, he died in prison, reportedly after a plot to burn the city to escape (Livy 34.44).

people.name: Gaius Cornelius Cethegus
people.summary: Consul 197 who split the Cenomani from the Insubres and won at the Mincius, triumphing with Hamilcar the Carthaginian among his captives; he vowed the temple of Juno Sospita. As censor 194 he gave senators separate seats at the games.

people.name: Lucius Furius Purpurio
people.summary: As praetor in 200 he defeated the Gauls who had sacked Placentia outside Cremona, killing the Carthaginian Hamilcar (in one version) and triumphing without his army. Consul 196, a commissioner at Apamea in 188, and a critic of Manlius Vulso.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
people.summary: Son of the great Marcellus, who escaped the ambush that killed his father in 208. He dedicated the temple of Honos and Virtus in 205, triumphed as consul over the Insubres and Comum in 196, and was censor in 189 with Titus Flamininus.

people.name: Lucius Quinctius Flamininus
people.summary: Brother of Titus; commanded the fleet in the Second Macedonian War and took Eretria. Consul 192. In 184 Cato expelled him from the Senate for killing a Gallic deserter (in another version a condemned man) at dinner in Gaul to amuse a favourite who had never seen a man killed.

people.name: Quintus Minucius Thermus
people.summary: Won a victory at Turda in Spain (196) and fought the Ligurians from Pisae for four years after his consulship (193-190). Cato attacked him in two speeches, one charging that he had flogged ten Ligurian magistrates for poor supplies. He was killed in Thrace in 188 when Thracians ambushed Manlius Vulso's returning army.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Regillus
people.summary: Praetor 190 who with the Rhodians destroyed Polyxenidas' fleet at Myonessus, opening the sea route for the Scipios. He triumphed at sea in 189 and vowed a temple to the Lares Permarini, dedicated in 179 with a tablet recording the victory.

people.name: Gaius Livius Salinator
people.summary: Commander of the Roman fleet in 191 who, with Eumenes II, defeated Polyxenidas off Corycus and crossed into the Hellespont. Consul 188. A kinsman of the victor of the Metaurus.

people.name: Spurius Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 186 who, warned by Hispala Faecenia and Aebutius, laid the Bacchic conspiracy before the Senate and ran the inquiry that followed throughout Italy. In 185-184 he also uncovered slave conspiracies among Apulian herdsmen. He died in the epidemic of 180.

people.name: Quintus Marcius Philippus
people.summary: Consul 186, when he lost 4,000 men in the Ligurian 'Saltus Marcius'. As envoy in 172 he lulled Perseus with a truce while Rome prepared, a trick older senators condemned as 'new wisdom' (nova sapientia). As consul again in 169, aged about 60, he forced the passes into Pieria. Censor 164.

people.name: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Victor over the Celtiberians at Aebura and in the Manlian pass (181-180), when he vowed the temple of Fortuna Equestris. As censor in 174 he stripped half the marble roof tiles from Juno Lacinia at Croton for his temple; the Senate ordered them returned. Hearing that one son had died and another was dying in Illyria, he hanged himself in 172.

people.name: Gaius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: Consul 177 who finished the Istrian war at Nesactium and recaptured Mutina from the Ligurians. As censor in 169 with Tiberius Gracchus he was prosecuted by the tribune Publius Rutilius; eight of the twelve centuries of the first class voted to convict before Gracchus' oath to share his fate turned the vote.

people.name: Quintus Petillius Spurinus
people.summary: As urban praetor in 181 he examined the 'Books of Numa' found on the Janiculum and had them burned in the Comitium. As consul 176 he was killed attacking the Ligurians on Mons Letum, having (Livy says) remarked before the battle that he would 'take Letum', an omen on the word letum, death.
people.death: killed in battle with the Ligurians

people.name: Lucius Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 173 who, angry at a past slight from Praeneste, ordered the town to receive him with lodging, transport and a public welcome when he went to sacrifice at the shrine of Fortuna. Livy marks it as the first time a Roman magistrate imposed such burdens on allies, and a precedent that grew.

people.name: Marcus Popillius Laenas
people.summary: Consul 173 who attacked the Ligurian Statellates, who had not fought Rome, and sold 10,000 of them after their surrender. He defied the Senate's order to free them and was shielded by his brother, consul in 172, and by delays in the inquiry voted by plebiscite. Censor 159.

people.name: Publius Licinius Crassus
people.summary: Consul 171, first commander against Perseus. His cavalry and light infantry were beaten near the hill of Callinicus outside Larissa; he spent the rest of the year plundering Boeotian and Thessalian allies and was later accused of extortion.

people.name: Gaius Lucretius Gallus
people.summary: Praetor 171 in command of the fleet, who sacked Haliartus and plundered Chalcis and other allied towns. In 170 two tribunes prosecuted him on the complaint of the Chalcidians, and all 35 tribes condemned him to a fine of a million asses.

people.name: Aulus Hostilius Mancinus
people.summary: Consul 170 whose year against Perseus produced no result. On his way to the army through Epirus he narrowly escaped a plot by the Molossian leaders Theodotus and Philostratus to hand him over to the Macedonians.

people.name: Gnaeus Octavius
people.summary: Praetor 168 who blockaded Perseus on Samothrace and took his surrender, triumphing at sea and building the Porticus Octavia with its bronze capitals. Consul 165, the first of his family. Sent to Syria to enforce the Apamea limits, he burned ships and hamstrung the Seleucid elephants and was murdered at Laodicea in 162; the Senate set up his statue on the Rostra.

people.name: Gaius Sulpicius Galus
people.summary: Aemilius Paullus' military tribune who, on the eve of Pydna (21 June 168), told the troops that a lunar eclipse was coming and why, so that they were not alarmed. Consul 166, triumphing over the Ligurians; Cicero presents him as Rome's first serious astronomer.

people.name: Quintus Fulvius Nobilior
people.summary: Consul 153, the first to take office on 1 January for the Spanish emergency. He was ambushed on the feast of the Vulcanalia by the Segedans under Carus, losing 6,000 citizens, and his elephants stampeded before Numantia. Patron of Ennius, to whom his father gave citizenship.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
people.summary: Grandson of the hero of Syracuse; consul three times (166, 155, 152), the third time against the custom that led to the ban on iteration. In Spain he founded Corduba and negotiated a moderate peace with the Celtiberians in 152-151. He drowned in a storm on an embassy to Masinissa in 148.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus
people.summary: Consul 148 who took over the stalled siege of Carthage, failed against Clupea and Hippo Diarrhytus and achieved nothing, which fed the popular demand for Scipio Aemilianus. Earlier, as praetor in Ulterior in 154, he had been beaten by the Lusitanians.

people.name: Gaius Vetilius
people.summary: Praetor in Hispania Ulterior who had surrounded a Lusitanian force and was negotiating its settlement when Viriathus took command. Lured into the defile of Tribola in 147, his army was cut to pieces; an old and fat man, he was captured and killed by a soldier who did not recognise him.
people.death: killed after the defeat at Tribola

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus
people.summary: Eldest son of Aemilius Paullus, adopted into the Fabii Maximi, and brother of Scipio Aemilianus. He fought at Pydna and as consul in 145 took raw levies to Spain, trained them for a season, and in 144 drove Viriathus back and took two of his towns.

people.name: Quintus Pompeius
people.summary: A new man who won the consulship of 141 against Laelius, having promised Scipio Aemilianus not to stand. At Numantia he lost men in repeated failures, then in 140/139 made a secret treaty with the Numantines for a payment of 30 talents, which he denied before the Senate when his successor arrived. Censor 131, the first plebeian censor pair.

people.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina
people.summary: Consul 137, sent to replace Mancinus. Wanting glory, he attacked the Vaccaei and besieged Pallantia in 136 despite the Senate's envoys forbidding it; he retreated in disorder, losing 6,000 men, and was stripped of command and fined. Cicero rated him the first Roman orator to use smooth periodic style.

people.name: Lucius Furius Philus
people.summary: Consul 136 who handed the naked, bound Mancinus over to the Numantines, who refused him. A friend of Scipio Aemilianus and Laelius and a learned Hellenist, he speaks in Cicero's De re publica, where he argues Carneades' case against justice.

people.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: Consul 143 who attacked the Alpine Salassi, triumphed without senatorial approval, and was protected from a tribune's veto by his Vestal daughter riding in his chariot. Censor 136 and princeps senatus, rival of Scipio Aemilianus, father-in-law of Tiberius Gracchus and member of the agrarian commission of 133.

people.name: Quintus Marcius Rex
people.summary: Praetor 144 entrusted by the Senate with 180 million sesterces to repair the Aqua Appia and Anio Vetus and to build a new aqueduct; his command was prorogued to finish the Aqua Marcia, which he carried to the Capitol despite objections from the decemviri sacris faciundis.

people.name: Lucius Hostilius Tubulus
people.summary: Praetor 142 who presided over a murder court and took bribes so openly that in 141 a special quaestio was voted against him on the tribune Publius Mucius Scaevola's bill. He went into exile and, recalled to stand trial, took poison. Cicero uses him as a byword for judicial corruption.

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 151 (when he and Lucullus were imprisoned by tribunes over the levy) and author of a Roman history in Greek. In its preface he begged pardon for errors in a foreign tongue; Cato asked who had compelled him to write in Greek. Polybius thought him a vain Hellenomaniac.

people.name: Lucius Cincius Alimentus
people.summary: Praetor 210, then commander in Sicily, who was captured by Hannibal and, as he wrote, heard from Hannibal himself that 36,000 men had been lost crossing from the Rhône to Italy. He wrote a history of Rome in Greek from the foundation, which he dated to 729/8 BC.

people.name: Gaius Acilius
people.summary: Senator who interpreted for the Athenian philosophers before the Senate in 155 and wrote a history of Rome in Greek, later translated into Latin by one Claudius. Livy cites him for the conference between Hannibal and Scipio at Ephesus.

people.name: Naevius

roles.t: Soldier in the First Punic War

people.summary: Campanian-born poet, veteran of the First Punic War, author of comedies, tragedies, the first Roman historical plays (fabulae praetextae such as Clastidium) and the Bellum Punicum in Saturnian verse. His jibes at the Metelli ('fato Metelli Romae fiunt consules') reportedly brought prison and exile; he died at Utica.

people.name: Caecilius Statius
people.summary: An Insubrian Gaul enslaved as a boy, perhaps in the wars of the 190s, freed and active as a writer of comedies after Plautus, adapting Menander. Volcacius Sedigitus ranked him first of Roman comic poets. He died the year after Ennius and was buried near him on the Janiculum.

people.name: Pacuvius
people.summary: Nephew of Ennius from Brundisium, painter (a work of his hung in the temple of Hercules in the Forum Boarium) and the leading Roman tragedian between Ennius and Accius. He wrote a praetexta, Paullus, and tragedies such as Dulorestes and Iliona. In 140 he and the young Accius staged plays at the same games; he retired to Tarentum.

people.name: Lucius Cassius Hemina
people.summary: The first known annalist to write Roman history in Latin prose on a large scale after Cato, writing around 146 (he mentions the fourth Secular Games, which he dated to 146). Fragments survive chiefly through Pliny and the grammarians, including the arrival of the first Greek doctor, Archagathus, in 219.

people.name: Sextus Aelius Paetus Catus
people.summary: Consul 198 and censor 194, the jurist Ennius called 'egregie cordatus homo'. His Tripertita set out the Twelve Tables, their interpretation and the legis actiones, and was called the 'cradle of the law' (cunabula iuris) by Pomponius.

people.name: Gaius Licinius Crassus
people.summary: Tribune 145 who proposed that vacancies in the priestly colleges be filled by popular election instead of co-option. Laelius' speech on the antiquity of the pontifical rites defeated the bill. Cicero says Crassus was the first to address the people facing the Forum rather than the Comitium and Curia.

people.name: Hieronymus
people.summary: Grandson and successor of Hiero II, aged fifteen. Led by his uncles Andranodorus and Zoippus and the Carthaginian agents Hippocrates and Epicydes, he broke with Rome and negotiated with Carthage for all Sicily. After thirteen months he was assassinated at Leontini in 214; his family was then massacred.

people.name: Hippocrates
people.summary: Born at Carthage to a Syracusan exile and a Carthaginian mother, he served with Hannibal in Italy and was sent with his brother Epicydes to Hieronymus. Elected general after the king's murder, he broke the Roman alliance, provoked Marcellus at Leontini, held the field against him in the siege and died of plague in the Carthaginian camp in 212.

people.name: Epicydes
people.summary: Brother of Hippocrates, also raised at Carthage and an officer of Hannibal. He commanded inside Syracuse during the siege, escaped to Agrigentum before the fall of Achradina in 212 and fled to Carthage when Agrigentum was betrayed in 210.

people.name: Antigonus III Doson
people.summary: Guardian of the young Philip V who took the royal title, rebuilt Macedonian power, and at Aratus' invitation intervened in the Peloponnese against Cleomenes III, forming the Hellenic Symmachy (224) and winning at Sellasia (222). He died after defeating an Illyrian invasion in 221.

people.name: Aratus of Sicyon

roles.t: Strategos of the Achaean League (17 times)

people.summary: Liberator of Sicyon (251), who brought it into the Achaean League and made the League the main power of the Peloponnese, seizing Acrocorinth from Macedon in 243. Threatened by Cleomenes III, he reversed his life's policy and called in Antigonus Doson. Adviser to Philip V, he was alienated by Philip's turn west and, according to Polybius and Plutarch, slowly poisoned by him. His memoirs were a source for Polybius.
people.death: believed poisoned on Philip V's orders

people.name: Cleomenes III
people.summary: Spartan king who in 227 killed the ephors, cancelled debts and redistributed land, enlarged the citizen body and nearly broke the Achaean League. Defeated at Sellasia in 222 by Antigonus Doson, he fled to Ptolemy III and, held at Alexandria under Ptolemy IV, died in a failed rising in 219.
people.death: suicide during a failed coup in Alexandria

people.name: Seleucus IV Philopator
people.summary: Son of Antiochus III, who commanded at Magnesia and inherited a kingdom burdened by the Apamea indemnity. He sent his chancellor Heliodorus to seize the Jerusalem temple treasure and exchanged his son Demetrius as hostage for his brother Antiochus. Heliodorus murdered him in 175.

people.name: Ptolemy V Epiphanes
people.summary: Child king whose regents lost Coele-Syria to Antiochus III at Panium (200). Crowned at Memphis in 196, an event commemorated by the decree on the Rosetta Stone, he married Antiochus' daughter Cleopatra I in 194/3 and crushed the Theban revolt in 186. He died, perhaps poisoned, in 180.

people.name: Ptolemy VI Philometor
people.summary: Son of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I. Defeated and captured by Antiochus IV in 170-169, he was saved by Popillius at Eleusis. Expelled by his brother Ptolemy VIII, he came to Rome in 164 dressed as a commoner. Restored, he ruled a strong Egypt until he died of wounds after defeating Alexander Balas near Antioch in 145.
people.death: died of wounds after the battle of the Oenoparas

people.name: Cleopatra I Syra
people.summary: Daughter of Antiochus III, married to Ptolemy V at Raphia in winter 194/3 with a dowry that, Ptolemaic courtiers later claimed, included Coele-Syria's revenues. As regent for Ptolemy VI she kept peace with her brother Seleucus IV; the first Ptolemaic queen to issue coins in her own name.

people.name: Sosibius
people.summary: The minister who dominated Ptolemy IV's court, organised the murders of the king's mother, brother and uncle, and trained the native Egyptian phalanx that won Raphia (217). With Agathocles he concealed the king's death in 204 and had Queen Arsinoe III killed.

people.name: Scopas
people.summary: Aetolian leader who began the Social War of 220 and later, as a mercenary captain in Ptolemaic service, recruited 6,000 Aetolians and reconquered Judaea, only to be routed by Antiochus III at Panium (200) and forced to surrender in Sidon. Plotting a coup in Alexandria, he was executed in 196.

people.name: Achaeus
people.summary: Cousin of Antiochus III who restored Seleucid rule in Asia Minor against Attalus I, then took the diadem at Laodicea in 220. Besieged in the acropolis of Sardis from 215/4, he was betrayed by the Cretan Bolis, captured, mutilated and executed in 213.

people.name: Molon
people.summary: Satrap of Media who revolted against the young Antiochus III in 222, took Seleucia-on-the-Tigris and defeated royal armies. In 220 Antiochus met him in Apolloniatis; Molon's left wing went over to the king, and he killed himself; his body was impaled on the Zagros pass.

people.name: Demetrius
people.summary: Younger son of Philip V, a hostage in Rome after Cynoscephalae. Sent back in 184/3 to answer complaints, he was so well received by the Senate, which said it pardoned Philip for Demetrius' sake, that his brother Perseus could paint him as Rome's candidate for the throne. Philip had him poisoned in 180, reportedly on forged evidence.

people.name: Prusias I
people.summary: Bithynian king who fought Byzantium (220) and Pergamon, allied with Philip V and was rewarded with Cius and Myrlea. He sheltered Hannibal, who commanded his fleet against Eumenes II and, Nepos says, threw jars full of snakes onto the enemy decks. Under Roman pressure Prusias agreed to surrender Hannibal in 183.

people.name: Prusias II
people.summary: Married Perseus' sister but stayed neutral in the Third Macedonian War; in 167 he appeared before the Senate with shaven head and a freedman's cap, greeting it as 'saviour gods'. He invaded Pergamon in 156, sacking temples, until Rome forced peace and reparations (154). His son Nicomedes, aided by Attalus II, overthrew and killed him in 149.
people.death: killed at Nicomedia on his son's orders

people.name: Attalus II Philadelphus
people.summary: Brother and loyal general of Eumenes II, at Magnesia and in the Galatian wars. In Rome in 167 senators tempted him to ask for part of his brother's kingdom; he declined. As king he survived Prusias II's invasion, helped Rome against Andriscus and at Corinth, founded Attaleia and gave Athens the Stoa of Attalus.

people.name: Pharnaces I
people.summary: Pontic king who seized Sinope in 183, making it his capital, and fought Eumenes II, Ariarathes IV and Prusias II until compelled by Roman envoys and military pressure to accept peace in 179, giving up his gains in Galatia and Paphlagonia. Grandfather of Mithridates VI.

people.name: Callicrates
people.summary: Achaean politician who in 180 urged the Senate to back its friends in Greek states and so created, in Polybius' view, the class of informers who served Rome. After Pydna he denounced about 1,000 Achaeans, Polybius among them, who were deported to Italy. Hated at home, he died in 149 on an embassy to Rome.

people.name: Aristaenus
people.summary: Achaean strategos in 199/8 who persuaded the League at Sicyon to leave Philip V for Rome, and the leading advocate of compliance with Roman wishes in rivalry with Philopoemen, whose policy of defending Achaean rights within the alliance he opposed.

people.name: Lycortas
people.summary: Philopoemen's political heir and the father of Polybius. As strategos in 183/2 he avenged Philopoemen by capturing Messene and punishing his killers. In the Third Macedonian War he advocated strict neutrality, which put his circle, including his son, on Callicrates' list.

people.name: Polyxenidas
people.summary: Rhodian exile who commanded Antiochus III's Aegean fleet. Beaten off Corycus (191), he destroyed the Rhodian squadron of Pausistratus at Panormus on Samos by a feigned negotiation (190), but lost the decisive battle of Myonessus to Regillus and the Rhodians later that year.

people.name: Hannibal the Rhodian
people.summary: Carthaginian noble whose fast ship repeatedly ran the Roman blockade of Lilybaeum in broad daylight, taunting the Romans. He was finally caught by a captured four-banked ship of fine build; the Romans then used his vessel as the model for the fleet that won the Aegates.

people.name: Spendius
people.summary: A Campanian slave who had deserted from Rome to Carthaginian service and, fearing extradition, became with the Libyan Mathos the leader of the mercenary revolt. He ordered the torture and murder of Gesco and 700 prisoners, was trapped at the Saw and crucified before Tunis.

people.name: Gesco
people.summary: Carthaginian commander at Lilybaeum who after the peace shipped the army home in detachments, a prudent arrangement the authorities wrecked by concentrating the men at Sicca unpaid. Sent to negotiate with the mutineers at Tunis, he was seized, and in 239 he and some 700 others were mutilated and buried alive.
people.death: tortured to death by the mercenaries

people.name: Himilco
people.summary: Commander of the Carthaginian army of some 25,000 foot, 3,000 horse and 12 elephants that landed at Heraclea Minoa in 213, took Agrigentum and won over many Sicilian towns. He died with much of his army in the plague that swept the marshy camp outside Syracuse in 212.

people.name: Muttines
people.summary: A Libyphoenician of Hippo Acra trained under Hannibal, whose Numidian horse ravaged Roman Sicily from Agrigentum. Slighted by the jealous Carthaginian general Hanno, he betrayed Agrigentum to Laevinus in 210, received Roman citizenship as Marcus Valerius Muttines, and is honoured with his sons in a Delphic inscription of 190.

people.name: Gulussa
people.summary: Son of Masinissa, envoy to Rome in 172 and 168, and commander of the Numidian cavalry for Scipio Aemilianus in the Third Punic War. On Masinissa's death Aemilianus divided the royal functions, giving Gulussa command of the army; with Laelius he destroyed the Carthaginian field force at Nepheris.

people.name: Scerdilaidas
people.summary: Illyrian chieftain, brother or kinsman of Agron, who led the land army in 230 and later ruled the Ardiaean kingdom. He switched between Philip V and Rome, joining the Roman-Aetolian coalition in 211; with his son Pleuratus he was named among Rome's adherents in the Peace of Phoenice.

people.name: Alexander Balas
people.summary: A youth from Smyrna presented as a son of Antiochus IV, promoted by Attalus II and the Seleucid exile Heraclides and recognised by the Roman Senate in 153/2. With Ptolemy VI and Jonathan Maccabaeus he defeated and killed Demetrius I in 150, married Cleopatra Thea, lost Ptolemy's support and was killed fleeing after the battle of the Oenoparas in 145.

people.name: Panaetius
people.summary: Rhodian Stoic who joined Scipio Aemilianus' household around 144, accompanied him on his eastern embassy of 140-139, and adapted Stoic ethics to Roman aristocratic life; his On Duties was the model for Cicero's De officiis. He succeeded Antipater as head of the Stoa at Athens.

people.name: Crates of Mallos

roles.t: Envoy of Attalus II to Rome

people.summary: Stoic scholar and head of the library at Pergamon, rival of Aristarchus, who built a terrestrial globe. Sent to Rome as envoy (Suetonius dates it to the time of Ennius' death, c. 168), he broke his leg in an opening of the Cloaca Maxima on the Palatine and, while convalescing, gave lectures that Suetonius calls the beginning of grammatical studies at Rome.

people.name: Hampsicora
people.summary: Sardo-Punic magnate, the most powerful man in Sardinia, who raised the island against Rome after Cannae and called in Carthaginian help. His son Hostus lost a battle to Manlius Torquatus near Cornus; Hampsicora killed himself when the joint Sardinian-Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal the Bald was destroyed.

people.name: Hispala Faecenia
people.summary: A freedwoman and courtesan who, having been initiated as a slave, revealed the Bacchic rites to the consul Postumius to save her lover Aebutius. The Senate rewarded her with 100,000 asses and extraordinary legal rights, including the right to marry a freeborn man without disgrace.

people.name: Claudia Quinta

roles.t: Matron at the reception of the Magna Mater

people.summary: Noblewoman who, in Livy, was one of the matrons who received the sacred stone of the Magna Mater at Ostia in 204. Later tradition (Ovid, Suetonius) has her, accused of unchastity, single-handedly drawing the grounded ship upriver to prove her purity; her statue stood in the goddess' temple vestibule.

people.name: Aemilia Tertia
people.summary: Daughter of Lucius Aemilius Paullus (killed at Cannae), wife of Scipio Africanus and mother of Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi. Polybius describes the splendour of her processions; she knowingly tolerated her husband's affair with a slave girl, whom she freed after his death. Her estate passed to Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Chiomara

roles.t: Wife of the Tolistobogian chief Orgiagon

people.summary: Wife of a Galatian chieftain captured in Manlius Vulso's campaign of 189. Raped by a centurion who then sold her ransom back, she had her countrymen behead him at the exchange and threw the head at her husband's feet. Polybius met her later at Sardis and admired her intelligence.
